To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) we detected seven submillimeter sources in the COSMUS field, and (2) the radio-dim sources are likely to be high-redshift starbursts.
the radio-dimmest submillimeter galaxies are the most luminous, the most dust-obscured, and the highest redshift.
the radio-dims are more distant, more luminous, and more highly obscured than radio-bright submillimeter galaxies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of high redshift galaxies, in particular the submm galaxies.
the study of the evolution of galaxies in clusters and in the field.
the study of the formation of massive galaxies at high redshifts (z>2).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there exists a population of very luminous star-forming galaxies at z ~ 2-3, which have not yet been detected by optical surveys and are selected in the submillimeter.
the radio-dims appear to be the high- z analogs of local ULIRGs.
we have found evidence for a population of high- z starbursts, which are likely to be very dusty and have high IR luminosities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
submillimeter-selected galaxies are not a uniform population, but rather consist of at least two subpopulations with very different properties.
radio-bright and radio-quiet submillimeter galaxies are different populations.
the high-redshift submillimeter galaxy population has a bimodal radio spectral index distribution, with a radio-loud and radio-quiet component.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the submillimeter galaxy population is not a monolithic entity but instead contains multiple subpopulations with different characteristics.
the submillimeter galaxies in the COSMUS field are not a single, uniform population.
the radio-dimming phenomenon, previously observed at lower redshifts, is also present in the population of submillimeter galaxies at higher redshift.
